Mount Gilead
GIL-ee-uhd
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Gilad; the highland region east of the Jordan, the setting of Jacob's covenant with Laban and Gideon's winnowing of his army.

📖 Biblical Definition

Mount Gilead, or the highland of Gilead, was a fertile, mountainous region east of the Jordan, the scene of several significant events. There Jacob, fleeing from Laban, was overtaken; the two made a covenant of peace and raised a heap of stones as a witness, calling it Mizpah, "The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another" (Gen 31:49). Gilead was famed for its balm, a healing resin (Jer 8:22, "Is there no balm in Gilead?"). And it was "from mount Gilead" that Gideon, by the LORD's command, sent home the fearful from his army, that the deliverance might plainly be God's: "Whosoever is fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead. And there returned of the people twenty and two thousand; and there remained ten thousand" (Judg 7:3), and then God reduced them further to three hundred. Mount Gilead stands in the dictionary as the highland of covenant and of God's winnowing, a witness to the watchful LORD who keeps covenant between His people, to the famed balm that pictures the healing found only in God, and to the divine pattern of saving by the few, that no flesh might glory but the glory be the LORD's alone.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The highland east of the Jordan; setting of Jacob and Laban's covenant at Mizpah (Gen 31), famed for its healing balm (Jer 8:22), and where Gideon sent home the fearful from his army (Judg 7:3).

MOUNT GILEAD, proper noun. A fertile highland region east of the Jordan.

Where Jacob and Laban made a covenant at Mizpah (Gen 31:49).

Famed for its healing balm (Jer 8:22).

Where Gideon sent home the fearful from his army (Judg 7:3).

Where God reduced Gideon's force, that the victory might be His.

📖 Key Scripture

Gen 31:49 — "And Mizpah; for he said, The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another."

Judg 7:3 — "Now therefore go to, proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, Whosoever is fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead. And there returned of the people twenty and two thousand; and there remained ten thousand."

Jer 8:22 — "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?"

1 Cor 1:29 — "That no flesh should glory in his presence."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Mount Gilead needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the watchful, covenant-keeping LORD, the healing found only in God, and the divine pattern of saving by the few.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's saving by the few, that He alone may be glorified. At Gilead, Gideon's army was winnowed from twenty-two thousand to ten thousand to three hundred, lest Israel "vaunt themselves... saying, Mine own hand hath saved me" (Judg 7:2). The dictionary holds that God often reduces His people's strength to magnify His own, that no flesh should glory in His presence (1 Cor 1:29); the victories of faith are won not by numbers but by the LORD.

Balm-of-Gilead note. Gilead's famed balm became, in the prophet's lament, an image of a healing that the sin-sick nation would not seek: "Is there no balm in Gilead?" (Jer 8:22). The dictionary holds the deeper truth the image points to: there is a balm for the wounded soul, but it is found in God alone and supremely in Christ the great Physician; the tragedy is not the lack of remedy but the refusal of the sinner to come and be healed.
